cards.title: Mark Steward
cards.sub: 2022 · FCA Executive Director of Enforcement and Market Oversight
cards.prompt: The notice Steward announced penalised TSB over the 2018 migration. Was the charge the technical failures customers hit, or something upstream of them?
cards.answer: Upstream. TSB was penalised for failing to organise and control the migration programme adequately and for failing to manage the operational risk of outsourcing it to Sabadell's subsidiary — planning, governance and supplier oversight. The outage was the harm; the plan was the offence.
cards.body: Steward ran FCA enforcement and was the FCA's named voice on the case. The Final Notice is dated 20 December 2022 - four years and eight months after the migration weekend it is about. Two regulators split the penalty: £29,750,000 to the FCA, £18,900,000 to the PRA, a combined £48,650,000.

cards.title: The Main Migration Event
cards.sub: 20–22 April 2018 · TSB Bank plc / Banco Sabadell
cards.prompt: TSB moved 5.2 million customers to a new core platform in one weekend. Name the single property of that cutover that turned every later bug into an eight-month incident.
cards.answer: It was irreversible - the FCA's word. To migrate at all TSB had to waive its right to keep the Lloyds platform, and after the data moved there was only a very short window before Lloyds disabled it. A roll-back plan, the FCA says, "was not possible", so every defect had to be fixed forward, live.
cards.body: TSB left Lloyds Banking Group's platform for Sabadell's Proteo4UK in a predominantly single-event 'big bang' weekend, going live on the Sunday. In week one, 20-30% of retail and business customers could not pay anyone online, and 26 were reading other customers' statements. Business as usual did not return until 10 December 2018.

cards.title: Final Notice to TSB Bank plc
cards.prompt: To argue the TSB case from evidence rather than press coverage, which public document lets you quote TSB's own board papers — and what are its reference number and date?
cards.answer: The FCA's Final Notice to TSB Bank plc, reference number 191240, dated 20 December 2022, free to download from fca.org.uk; a parallel PRA Final Notice covers the prudential side. It quotes TSB's internal plans verbatim, including the plan 'created on a top-down and right-to-left basis'.
cards.body: An agreed statement of facts, published in full. It runs to hundreds of numbered paragraphs covering 2015 to 2018: the Sabadell offer document, the board deep-dives, the dress rehearsals, the go-live assurance memo, the complaint counts, and the £32,705,762 paid in redress. Regulators write the post-mortems banks do not publish.

cards.title: Why reads flip before writes
cards.prompt: The four phases each buy back one rollback. Price the window: at exactly which moment does it shut, and what does going back cost either side of it?
cards.answer: It shuts at the first write the new store holds and the old one never saw. Before that the old store is still authoritative and still being written, so going back costs a feature flag. After it, going back costs customer money. That is the whole reason writes flip last and the old store keeps taking them for weeks after reads have moved.
cards.body: TSB is not this pattern failing, it is the case where the pattern was off the table: the old platform belonged to Lloyds and migrating meant signing away the right to keep it, so no ordering of deploys bought a way back. Cross-owner stores are the kernel's own break case.
